parts.latex: The derivative of $y=\sin x^\circ$ is

solutions.latex:
Convert degrees to radians: $x^\circ = \dfrac{\pi x}{180}$ radians, so $y = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)$.

By the chain rule,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}x\right)$$

parts.latex: If $f(x)=\tan\left(g\left(x^2\right)\right)$, where $g(x)$ is a differentiable function, what is $f'(x)$?

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule (twice):
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=\sec^2\left(g(x^2)\right)\times\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(g(x^2)\right)\\ &=\sec^2\left(g(x^2)\right)\times g'(x^2)\times 2x\\ &=2x\,g'(x^2)\sec^2\left(g(x^2)\right) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $y=3\cos(4x)$?

solutions.latex:
Differentiating, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos ax=-a\sin ax$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3\cos(4x)\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-12\sin(4x)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\cos(\ln x)$, where $x>0$?

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\cos(\ln x)\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=-\sin(\ln x)\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln x)\\ &=-\sin(\ln x)\times\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=-\dfrac{\sin(\ln x)}{x}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\tan(\ln x)$, where $x>0$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln x=\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan u=\sec^2 u$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\tan(\ln x) &= \dfrac{1}{x}\sec^2(\ln x) \\ &= \dfrac{\sec^2(\ln x)}{x} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: If $f(x) = \cos x$, the value of $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is,

solutions.latex:
The derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$.
$$f'(x) = -\sin x$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $y = \tan\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan(ax) = a\sec^2(ax)$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{3}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: Show that the function $f(x) = \sin 2x - 3x$ is decreasing throughout its domain.
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$f'(x)=2\cos 2x-3$$
Since $-1\le\cos 2x\le 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} -2&\le 2\cos 2x\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\\ -5&\le 2\cos 2x-3\le -1 &&(\text{subtract } 3)\end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)<0$ for all $x$.

$\therefore$ $f(x)$ is decreasing throughout its domain.

parts.latex: Given $f(x) = \cos(e^x)$, what of the following is the correct expression for $f'(x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with inner function $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= -\sin(e^x)\times e^x \\ &= -e^x\sin(e^x) \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Which of the following is the derivative of $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ with respect to $x$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin x & v&=\cos x\\ u'&=\cos x & v'&=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{\cos x\cos x - (-\sin x)\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\operatorname{cosec}(x)$?

solutions.latex:
Write $\operatorname{cosec} x=(\sin x)^{-1}$ and apply the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -(\sin x)^{-2}\times\cos x \\ &= \dfrac{-\cos x}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: What is the value of the derivative of $y = 2\sin 3x - 3\tan x$ at $x = 0$?

solutions.latex:
Differentiating each term,
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2(3)\cos 3x - 3\sec^2 x$$
At $x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 6\cos 0 - 3\sec^2 0 \\ &= 6 - 3 \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: What is $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}+h\right)-\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)}{h}$?

solutions.latex:
The limit is the definition of the derivative of $f(x)=\cos x$ at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
$$f'(x)=-\sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) &= -\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(4\tan\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}x\right)\right)$?

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan(kx)=k\sec^2(kx)$ with $k=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(4\tan\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}x\right)\right) &= 4\cdot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}x\right) \end{aligned}$$
Hence the correct option is B.

parts.latex: Which of the following is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=2\tan(3-2x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Use the chain rule with $\dfrac{d}{du}(\tan u)=\sec^2 u$ and $u=3-2x$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= 2\sec^2(3-2x)\times(-2) \\ &= -4\sec^2(3-2x) \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Prove $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)=-\operatorname{cosec}x\cot x$

solutions.latex:
Write $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=1 & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=0 & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{cosec}x)&=\dfrac{\sin x\times 0-\cos x}{(\sin x)^2}\\ &=-\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\ &=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct quotient rule derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $f(x)=4\sin 3x$, what is $f'(0)$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin 3x = 3\cos 3x$, so
$$f'(x)=12\cos 3x$$
Substituting $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(0) &= 12\cos 0 \\ &= 12 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex: If $f(x) = \tan\left(\sqrt{x}-2\right)$, what is $f'(x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule, with inner function $\sqrt{x}-2$ whose derivative is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$:
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^2\left(\sqrt{x}-2\right)$$
Hence option C.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{x}$. Show all working.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{x} &= 4\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4x} \\ &= 4\times 1 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\cos(\ln x)$, where $x>0$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule with $u=\ln x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos u = -\sin u\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(\ln x) &= -\sin(\ln x)\times\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sin(\ln x)}{x} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option A.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\sec x$ ?

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and differentiate:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec x) &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec x \tan x \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\sec x$.

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec x = (\cos x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)^{-1} &= -(\cos x)^{-2}\cdot(-\sin x) \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \tan x \sec x \end{aligned}$$
Hence the derivative of $\sec x$ is $\tan x \sec x$, which is option D.

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\text{cosec}^2 x$

solutions.latex:
Write $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ and use the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=-\sin x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x)&=\dfrac{-\sin x\cdot\sin x-\cos x\cdot\cos x}{\sin^2 x}\\ &=\dfrac{-(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)}{\sin^2 x}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x} &&(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1)\\ &=-\text{cosec}^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x)=-\text{cosec}^2 x$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule to $\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, or equivalent merit
